title: Oppenheimer recalls the Trinity test and the Bhagavad Gita

tellings.quote: I remembered the line from the Hindu scripture, the Bhagavad Gita. Now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds.
Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom, The Slayer Time, Ancient of Days, come hither to consume;

plain: When the first atomic bomb was exploded in the New Mexico desert in 1945, in what was called the Trinity test, the physicist who led the bomb's making, J. Robert Oppenheimer, says a line of Hindu scripture came into his mind. In a recording of his own words played on the show, he says: 'I remembered the line from the Hindu scripture, the Bhagavad Gita. Now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds.' The Bhagavad Gita is a sacred Hindu poem in which the god Krishna speaks to a warrior, and tradition credits it to the sage Vyasa. Oppenheimer does not say which translation his words follow, and he read the poem in Sanskrit. In Edwin Arnold's English translation of 1885, The Song Celestial, the same verse, chapter 11, verse 32, has Krishna say: 'Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom, The Slayer Time, Ancient of Days, come hither to consume.' So 'Now I am become death' is Oppenheimer's own rendering of that verse, with death where Arnold has Time. The line is told because it shows how the man who built the bomb understood what he had just let loose on the world.

discussion.by: The Song Celestial, or Bhagavad-Gita (translated by Edwin Arnold)
discussion.text: Oppenheimer does not say which translation his words follow, and he read the Gita in Sanskrit; in Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation read here, Krishna's words at chapter 11, verse 32 are "Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom", the same verse in another translator's English. "Now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds" is Oppenheimer's own rendering of it, with death where Arnold has Time.
